Inscribed Quadri

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a drawing, not a game: four special dots from a loop of four corners always sit on one straight line.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or D round the ring, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the dots, lines and circles, and press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

Four corners on a circle make four triangles. Each triangle has its own centre points, yet the four copies of each centre keep the same shape and their own centres fall neatly on one line. The boxes show the pieces one layer at a time.

One triangle, four centres

In any triangle the orthocenter H, the nine-point center N, the centroid G and the circumcenter O lie on the Euler line in that order. N is halfway from H to O and G is two thirds of the way: HN:NO = 1:1 and HG:GO = 2:1. With the Euler lines box ticked you can see all four lines pass through the common O.

Four triangles on one circle

For a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD the four triangles BCD, CDA, DAB and ABC share a circumcircle, so all four circumcentres are the same O. Write HA, NA, GA for the centres of BCD and so on. Tick Quadrilaterals and Homotheties: the three new quadrilaterals match ABCD, scaled by -1 for the H copy, -1/2 for the N copy and -1/3 for the G copy. Compared with each other about O, the H copy is three times the G copy and the N copy is 3/2 times it. These are homotheties.

The remarkable line

Each scaled copy has its own centre, H, N and G. The page's exact claim is that H, N, G and O are collinear and that HN:NO = 1:2 and HG:GO = 1:1 — different from the ratios inside one triangle. Put O at the origin and write the four corners as unit complex numbers a, b, c, d. The centre of the copy made with P(t) = t·(b+c+d) is Q(t) = t(a+b+c+d)/(1+t), so H = Q(1) = s/2, N = Q(1/2) = s/3 and G = Q(1/3) = s/4, where s = a+b+c+d. These three points and O lie at 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 of s, which gives the claimed ratios. The logic test checks them, and all the other claims above, on two thousand generated shapes.

One point, many lines

From NA = (b+c+d)/2 we get |H - NA| = |a|/2 = R/2: H is the circumcentre of the four nine-point centres, and all four nine-point circles pass through H. The Simson lines of the four corners also pass through H, as do the four maltitudes (perpendiculars from a side's midpoint to the opposite side) and the perpendicular from a diagonal's midpoint to the other diagonal — which is why H is called the anticenter. The test checks all four families of lines independently of the drawing code.

Tick Quadrilaterals and Homotheties, then drag one corner: the three copy shapes keep their sizes relative to ABCD while the line through H, N, G and O barely tilts.

The manifest's address for this applet pointed to a different cut-the-knot page about diagonal ratios; the applet itself is embedded on the "Remarkable Line in Cyclic Quadrilateral" page linked below. The applet's own info string still calls it "Pairs of incricles in a quadrilateral", a copied label with no counterpart in its code. Its nine checkbox names, starting angles, circle size and near-parallel safeguards are kept as they are; the modern look and the SVG handles are new.
